title: Bucket Words by Their Letters
statement:
Given a list of lowercase words, put words into the same group when one is a rearrangement of the other: same letters, same counts, any order. Return the list of groups.

Every input word appears in exactly one group, duplicates included. The order of the groups and the order of words inside a group do not matter.

examples.why: "sat" has no e, so it is not a rearrangement of "seat" and sits alone.
"aab" and "abb" use the same two letters but in different counts, so they are in different groups.
Empty words are rearrangements of each other, and both copies are kept.

constraints: words[i] contains only lowercase English letters
hints: Two words belong together when some key built from each word is the same. What key ignores letter order?
Sorting the letters of a word gives such a key. Then a hash map from key to list of words does the grouping.
Sorting each word costs k log k. A string of 26 letter counts is also a key and takes O(k) to build. Put a separator between the counts.

explain.intuition:
Grouping is a hash map job: compute a key for each word and push the word into the list stored under that key. The only question is the key. It must be equal for rearrangements and different for everything else.

The sorted letters of a word work: "vase", "save" and "aves" all become "aesv". A tally of how many a's, b's, … z's the word has works too and avoids sorting. It is the same idea as grouping API responses by a normalised cache key.
steps: Create an empty map from key to list of words.
For each word, build its key: the letters sorted, or the 26 letter counts joined with a separator.
Append the word to the list under that key, creating the list if needed.
Return all the lists in the map.
pitfalls: Using the sum of character codes as the key: "bc" and "ad" both sum to 197.
Joining the counts without a separator: counts [1, 11] and [11, 1] would both become "111".
Using the set of letters as the key: "aab" and "abb" would land in the same group.

complexity.time: O(n · k log k) with sorted keys, O(n · k) with count keys (k = word length)

solutions.title: Sorted letters as the key
solutions.idea: Rearrangements have the same sorted form, so use it as the map key.

solutions.title: Letter counts as the key
solutions.idea: Tally the 26 letters of each word and use the tally as the key. No sorting needed.

followups: Words can contain any Unicode characters. Which of the two keys still works, and what changes?
Return only the largest group. Can you avoid storing the other groups' words?
